introduction-kubernetes-the-aws-way.core: EKS runs upstream, conformant Kubernetes with an AWS-managed control plane, integrating Kubernetes concepts with AWS primitives: pods get VPC IPs, service accounts map to IAM roles, load balancers come from the AWS Load Balancer Controller, and nodes come from managed node groups, Karpenter or Fargate.

first_principles.problem: Self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 means running etcd, upgrades and HA control planes yourself.
truths: The control plane is hard to operate.
Kubernetes is portable; integrations are cloud-specific.
AWS identity and networking differ from Kubernetes defaults.

analogy.title: Leasing a managed office building
analogy.story: The landlord runs security, lifts and power; you furnish the floors.
analogy.breaks: Landlords rarely force renovations; EKS versions reach end of standard support and need upgrades.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: HA control plane and nodes in minutes.

code.text:
eksctl create cluster --name prod --region eu-west-1 --version 1.31 \
  --nodegroup-name system --node-type m7g.large --nodes 3 --managed

check.q: What part of Kubernetes does EKS manage for you?
check.a: The control plane: API servers, etcd and controllers, across multiple AZs.

managed-control-plane-architecture.core: Each EKS cluster's control plane runs in an AWS-owned VPC across three AZs: at least two API server instances behind a load balancer and a three-node etcd cluster, auto-scaled and patched by AWS. Worker nodes reach it through cross-account ENIs placed in your subnets, with public, private or both endpoint access.

first_principles.problem: Teams don't know why API access fails from inside the VPC after disabling the public endpoint.
truths: Control planes need HA and quorum.
Nodes need a network path to the API server.
Endpoint exposure is a security choice.

analogy.title: A bank's head office connected to branches by private lines
analogy.story: The head office runs elsewhere, but private lines reach into every branch.
analogy.breaks: Head offices are visible; the EKS control plane is opaque except through APIs and logs.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: API reachable only from the VPC (or connected networks).

check.q: How do worker nodes reach the EKS control plane?
check.a: Through cross-account ENIs that EKS places in your VPC subnets (or the public endpoint).

node-groups-managed-self-managed-and-far.core: EKS compute options: managed node groups (AWS-managed ASGs with graceful updates), self-managed nodes (full control over AMIs and bootstrap), Karpenter (flexible just-in-time nodes) and Fargate (a microVM per pod, no nodes to manage). Each trades control against operational effort.

first_principles.problem: A team spends days patching self-managed nodes when managed options would do.
truths: Node management is toil.
Some workloads need custom AMIs or GPUs.
Fargate has feature limits (no DaemonSets, no privileged pods).

analogy.title: Company cars: managed lease, owned fleet or taxis
analogy.story: Leased cars are maintained for you; owned cars give control; taxis need no garage at all.
analogy.breaks: Cars don't host each other; nodes run many pods, so blast radius differs.

example.title: Mixed cluster
flow: Managed group (3 × m7g.large) for CoreDNS, Karpenter
Fargate profile for untrusted batch jobs

check.q: Name one limitation of EKS Fargate.
check.a: No DaemonSets (also no privileged containers, no GPUs historically, no host networking).

pod-networking-the-vpc-cni-plugin.core: The Amazon VPC CNI gives each pod a real VPC IP from the node's subnet by attaching ENIs and secondary IPs to the node. Pods are first-class VPC citizens (security groups, flow logs, direct routing), but the number of pods per node is limited by ENIs × IPs per ENI, and subnets can run out of IPs.

first_principles.problem: A cluster can't schedule pods because the subnet ran out of IP addresses.
truths: Each pod consumes a VPC IP.
Instance types limit ENIs and IPs.
Warm pools pre-allocate IPs.
derivation: **Plan subnets** large (/19 or bigger) or use **secondary CIDRs** (100.64.0.0/10).

analogy.title: Giving every employee a real company phone extension
analogy.story: Calls route directly, but you can run out of extensions on a small switchboard.
analogy.breaks: Phone extensions are cheap to add; subnet sizes are fixed once created.

example.title: Max pods on m5.large
flow: Fix: secondary CIDR or prefix delegation

check.q: What limits the number of pods per node with the VPC CNI (without prefix delegation)?
check.a: The instance type's maximum ENIs and IPv4 addresses per ENI.

advanced-networking-prefix-delegation.core: Prefix delegation assigns /28 IPv4 prefixes (16 addresses) to ENI slots instead of single secondary IPs, multiplying pod density per node (e.g. 110+ pods on small instances) and speeding pod startup. It requires Nitro instances and subnets with contiguous free /28 blocks; IPv6 clusters avoid exhaustion entirely.

first_principles.problem: Small nodes cap at ~29 pods, wasting CPU and memory, and IP allocation slows pod startup.
truths: ENI slots are limited.
Each slot can hold a prefix instead of one IP.
Fragmented subnets may lack free /28s.
derivation: Use **fresh or defragmented subnets** (subnet CIDR reservations).

analogy.title: Assigning blocks of 16 seats instead of single seats per booking
analogy.story: Each reservation slot now covers a whole row.
analogy.breaks: Rows can be split later; prefixes must be contiguous free blocks.

code.text: kubectl set env daemonset aws-node -n kube-system ENABLE_PREFIX_DELEGATION=true WARM_PREFIX_TARGET=1

check.q: How many IPs does each /28 prefix provide?

eks-add-ons-managing-operational-softwar.core: EKS add-ons are AWS-managed installations of operational components (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS/EFS CSI drivers, Pod Identity Agent, observability agents) with versions validated per cluster version, lifecycle via API/IaC, and conflict-resolution settings for custom configuration.

first_principles.problem: After a cluster upgrade, an old CoreDNS or CNI version breaks networking.
truths: Core components must match the Kubernetes version.
Manual Helm installs drift.
Upgrades need ordering.

analogy.title: Manufacturer-approved parts for your car
analogy.story: Guaranteed to fit this model year and serviced by the dealer.
analogy.breaks: Car parts rarely change behaviour; add-on upgrades can change defaults, so read release notes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Compatible CoreDNS with custom config kept.

code.text:
aws eks describe-addon-versions --addon-name coredns --kubernetes-version 1.31
aws eks update-addon --cluster-name prod --addon-name coredns --addon-version v1.11.3-eksbuild.1 --resolve-conflicts PRESERVE

check.q: Why use managed add-ons for CoreDNS and the VPC CNI?
check.a: AWS validates compatible versions per Kubernetes release and manages their lifecycle, reducing upgrade breakage.

irsa-iam-roles-for-service-accounts.core: IRSA lets pods assume IAM roles through their Kubernetes service account: the cluster's OIDC provider signs a projected token, and STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity exchanges it for credentials scoped to that role. Each workload gets least-privilege AWS access without node-wide credentials. EKS Pod Identity is a newer, simpler alternative.

first_principles.problem: All pods on a node share the node's IAM role, so any compromised pod can access everything.
truths: Node roles are shared by all pods.
OIDC tokens can prove workload identity.
Trust policies can match service account names.
derivation: **Annotate** the service account with the role ARN.
SDKs pick up **web identity credentials** automatically.
Or use **Pod Identity associations**; block **IMDS** for pods.

analogy.title: Personal staff badges instead of one master key per floor
analogy.story: Each worker opens only the doors their job needs.
analogy.breaks: Badges are physical; tokens expire and rotate automatically.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only uploader pods can write to the media bucket.

code.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: uploader
  namespace: media
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/media-uploader

check.q: Why should you block pod access to the instance metadata service when using IRSA?
check.a: Otherwise pods could fall back to the node's IAM role credentials, bypassing least privilege.
